title: Collecting and Organising Data: Tables, Mode and Median
seo_title: Grade 6 Collecting and Organising Data Worksheets with Answers (CAPS Maths)
standard_text: Collect data using questionnaires (yes/no type questions and multiple-choice questions); organise data using tally marks, tables and stem-and-leaf displays; group data in intervals; summarise and distinguish between ungrouped numerical data by determining the mode and the median.
meta_desc: Free CAPS Grade 6 data handling worksheets: kinds of data, frequency tables, mode, median and range. 100 questions with memos.
key_big: Mode: most often. Median: middle when in order.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • Collect data with a questionnaire, tally marks or a table.
  • The mode is the value that appears most often.
  • The median is the middle value when the data is in order.
  • The range is the biggest value − the smallest value.

Examples

Example

Scores: 7, 3, 9, 7, 5

in order: 3, 5, 7, 7, 9

Answer: mode 7, median 7, range 6

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Median without orderingPut the data in order first.
The biggest valueThe mode is the most common.
The wrong rowUse a ruler to follow the row.

faq.q: What does CAPS Grade 6 say about data?
faq.a: Collect and organise data using tally marks, tables and stem-and-leaf displays, and summarise data using the mode and the median.

faq.q: What if there are two middle values?
faq.a: The median is halfway between them.
A table of each value and how often it appears.

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
Each learner’s favourite ice-cream flavour
items.e: The answers are names of flavours, so the data is categorical. Flavours have no natural order, so it is nominal.

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
The number of brothers and sisters each learner has
items.e: The answers are counted: 0, 1, 2, 3 … Counted data with only whole-number values is discrete. (Nobody has 2,5 brothers.)

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
Each learner’s height in centimetres
items.e: Height is measured, so it can be any value in a range, such as 148,6 cm. Measured data is continuous.

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
Shirt size: S, M, L or XL
items.e: The answers are categories that have a natural order: S is smaller than M, M is smaller than L. They are letters, not counts, so the data is not numerical.

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
The time each runner takes to run 100 m at the athletics day
items.e: Time is measured, and it can be any value, such as 15,37 seconds. So it is continuous numerical data.

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
How learners rate the tuck shop’s new wrap: poor, OK, good or excellent
items.e: The answers are words, so the data is categorical. Poor, OK, good, excellent have an order, so it is ordinal.

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
The way each learner gets to school: walk, bike, car or bus
items.e: The answers are categories with no natural order, so the data is nominal categorical.

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
The mass of each learner’s school bag in kilograms
items.e: Mass is measured, so it can be any value, such as 4,35 kg. Measured data is continuous numerical.

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
The place each swimmer finishes in a race: 1st, 2nd, 3rd …
items.e: The places are categories that tell the order the swimmers finished. They do not count or measure anything, so the data is ordinal categorical.

items.q:
What kind of data is this?
The number of learners on each school bus
items.e: Learners are counted, so the values are whole numbers only. The data is discrete numerical.

items.q:
Is this data discrete or continuous?
The number of pets each learner has
items.e: Pets are counted: 0, 1, 2, 3 … Nobody has 2,5 pets, so the data is discrete.

items.q:
Is this data discrete or continuous?
The height of each learner in centimetres
items.e: Height is measured. It can be any value in a range, such as 148,6 cm, so the data is continuous.

items.q:
Is this data discrete or continuous?
The time each learner takes to skate one lap of the rink
items.e: Time is measured. It can be 41 s, 41,3 s or 41,35 s, so the data is continuous.

items.q:
Is this data discrete or continuous?
The number of people in each canoe on a canoe trip
items.e: People are counted in whole numbers, so the data is discrete.

items.q:
Is this data discrete or continuous?
The number of loons counted on the lake each morning
items.e: Loons are counted in whole numbers, so the data is discrete.

items.q:
Is this data discrete or continuous?
The number of books each learner read over the summer holidays
items.e: Books are counted in whole numbers, so the data is discrete.

items.q: Which of these is continuous data?
items.e: Sleep is measured in time, so it can be 8,5 or 8,75 hours. The others are counted, so they are discrete.

items.q: Learners’ heights are grouped into intervals: 130 to 140 cm, 140 to 150 cm, and so on. Which graph fits best?
items.e: Height is continuous data. A histogram shows continuous data in equal intervals, with bars that touch.

items.q: Why do the bars of a histogram touch?
items.e: In a histogram, one interval ends where the next begins (140 cm is the end of one and the start of the next). There are no gaps in continuous data, so there are no gaps between the bars.

items.q: Which data is best shown on a broken-line graph?
items.e: A broken-line graph shows how continuous data changes over time. The puppy’s mass changes from week to week. The other data is categories, so a bar graph fits better.

items.q: Use the key. How many learners in 6B ride a bike?
items.e: 6B is the second (orange) column. The 6B column for Bike ends on the line between 8 and 10, so 9. (5 is 6A.)

items.q: How many learners in 6A come by car?
items.e: 6A is the first (green) column. The 6A column for Car reaches 10. (7 is 6B, and 17 is both classes.)

items.q: How many learners walk to school altogether, in both classes?
items.e: 6A: 8 walk. 6B: 4 walk. Altogether means add: 8 + 4 = 12. (4 subtracts instead of adds.)

items.q: How many more 6B learners than 6A learners ride a bike?
items.e: 6B: 9. 6A: 5. How many more means subtract: 9 − 5 = 4.

items.q: For which ways of travel does 6A have more learners than 6B?
items.e: Compare the two columns for each way. Walk: 8 and 4. Car: 10 and 7. In both, the green 6A column is taller. For bike and bus the orange 6B column is taller.

items.q: What is the mode for 6B?
items.e: The mode is the category with the tallest column. For 6B (orange) that is Bike, with 9 learners. The mode is the category, not the number 9. (Car is the mode for 6A.)

items.q: How many learners are in 6A?
items.e: Add all the 6A columns: 8 + 5 + 10 + 3 = 26. (10 is only the tallest column.)

items.q: Using both classes, which way of travel is the most common?
items.e: Add the two classes. Walk 12, bike 14, car 17, bus 9. Car is the most common. (Bike has the tallest single column, but you must add both classes.)

items.q: The scale is labelled in 10s. What is each small square worth?
items.e: There are 5 small squares between 0 and 10. 10 ÷ 5 = 2, so each small square is 2 drinks.

items.q: How many hot chocolates were sold in the week in July?
items.e: July is the orange column. The hot chocolate column reaches the line for 30. (4 is February, and 15 counts each small square as 1.)

items.q: How many bottles of water were sold in the week in February?
items.e: February is the green column. Water ends 2 small squares above 30. Each square is 2, so 30 + 4 = 34. (17 counts each small square as 1, and 16 is July.)

items.q: Which drinks sold more in the July week than in the February week?
items.e: The orange July column is taller for milk (18 and 12) and for hot chocolate (30 and 4). For water and juice, February is taller.

items.q: How many learners are at least 150 cm tall?
items.e: At least 150 cm means the bars from 150 to 160 and from 160 to 170: 12 + 5 = 17. (27 also adds the 140 to 150 bar.)

items.q: How many learners are shorter than 150 cm?
items.e: Shorter than 150 cm means the bars from 130 to 140 and from 140 to 150: 3 + 10 = 13. (10 is only one bar.)

items.q: Which interval has the median height?
items.e: There are 30 learners, so the median is between the 15th and 16th heights in order. The first two bars hold 3 + 10 = 13 learners, so the 14th to 25th learners are in the 150 to 160 bar.

items.q: What fraction of the learners are 160 cm or taller?
items.e: 5 of the 30 learners are in the 160 to 170 bar. 5 out of 30 = 1 out of 6. (1/5 comes from 5 out of 25, 2/5 reads the 150 to 160 bar (12 out of 30), and 1/4 counts the bars, not the learners.)

items.q: How tall was the sunflower in week 4?
items.e: Go up from week 4 to the point, then across: it is on the line for 40 cm.

items.q: How much did the sunflower grow from week 3 to week 4?
items.e: Week 3: 25 cm. Week 4: 40 cm. Growth = 40 − 25 = 15 cm. (40 is the height, not the growth.)

items.q: In which week did the sunflower grow the most?
items.e: The steepest part of the line shows the most growth. Week 5 to week 6: 75 − 55 = 20 cm. Every other week it grew 15 cm or less.

items.q: How much did the sunflower grow from week 1 to week 6?
items.e: Week 6: 75 cm. Week 1: 10 cm. 75 − 10 = 65 cm. (75 cm is its height, which includes the 10 cm it already had.)

items.q:
Ages of the children at a birthday party:
11, 12, 11, 10, 12, 11, 13
What is the mode?
items.e: 11 appears 3 times, more than any other age, so the mode is 11 years. (13 is the highest age, and 3 is how many times 11 appears.)

items.q:
Masses of 5 dogs at the vet (kg):
31, 25, 40, 28, 36
What is the range?
items.e: Highest 40 kg, lowest 25 kg. Range = 40 − 25 = 15 kg. (36 − 31 = 5 uses the last and first numbers, which are not the highest and lowest. 65 adds instead of subtracts.)

items.q: Each dot is one car. What is the mode?
items.e: The tallest stack is above 2, so the mode is 2 people. (9 is the number of cars, and 5 is the highest value.)

items.q: What is the range of the number of people in each car?
items.e: Range = highest − lowest = 5 − 1 = 4 people. Use the values along the number line, not the heights of the stacks (9 − 1 = 8).

items.q: Each dot is one learner. What is the mode?
items.e: The tallest stack (5 dots) is above 16, so the mode is 16. (5 is how many learners scored 16.)

items.q: What is the range of the scores?
items.e: Highest score 20, lowest score 12. Range = 20 − 12 = 8. (Nobody scored 13 or 19, but the range only uses the highest and lowest. 5 − 1 = 4 uses the heights of the stacks, and 32 adds.)

items.q:
Shoe sizes of 7 learners:
4, 5, 6, 5, 7, 6, 3
What is the mode?
items.e: 5 appears twice and 6 appears twice. Every other size appears once. So there are two modes: 5 and 6.

items.q:
Quiz scores of 5 learners:
3, 8, 6, 9, 4
What is the mode?
items.e: Each score appears only once, so no value appears most often. There is no mode. (9 is the highest score, and 5 is how many scores there are.)

items.q:
Long jump distances at the athletics day (m):
2,35; 2,8; 3,1; 2,62; 2,9
What is the range?
items.e: Highest 3,1 m, lowest 2,35 m. Line up the decimal points: 3,10 − 2,35 = 0,75 m. (2,9 − 2,35 = 0,55 uses the last value, not the highest.)

items.q:
Grade 6 voted for the end-of-year excursion.
ExcursionVotes
Zoo8
Beach11
Museum5
Movies10
What is the mode?
items.e: The mode is the category with the most votes. Beach has 11 votes. The mode is Beach, not the number 11.

items.q:
Grade 6 voted for the end-of-year excursion.
ExcursionVotes
Zoo8
Beach11
Museum5
Movies10
Thandi says, “The range of this data is 11 − 5 = 6.” What is wrong?
c: The places are categorical, so they have no range
items.e: The data is the place each learner chose. Places are nominal categories with no order, so there is no highest or lowest place. Range is only for numerical data.

items.q:
This table shows how many brothers and sisters the learners in 6D have.
Brothers and sistersLearners
05
111
27
32
51
What is the mode?
items.e: The most learners (11) have 1 brother or sister, so the mode is 1. (11 is the number of learners, and 5 is the highest value.)

items.q:
This table shows how many brothers and sisters the learners in 6D have.
Brothers and sistersLearners
05
111
27
32
51
What is the range of the data?
items.e: Highest value 5, lowest value 0. Range = 5 − 0 = 5. (11 − 1 = 10 uses the learner counts, and 5 − 1 = 4 forgets that 0 is a value.)

items.q: The range of 5 test scores is 12. The lowest score is 7. What is the highest score?
items.e: Range = highest − lowest, so highest = lowest + range = 7 + 12 = 19. (12 − 7 = 5 subtracts instead of adds, and 84 multiplies.)

items.q: One more car arrives with 3 people in it. What is the mode now?
items.e: Add one dot above 3: now 6 cars have 3 people. The tallest stack is still above 2 (9 dots), so the mode is still 2 people.

items.q: Which set of data has a range of 10?
items.e: Range = highest − lowest. 4, 14, 9, 7: 14 − 4 = 10. The others: 15 − 10 = 5, 11 − 3 = 8, 11 − 2 = 9. (Having the number 10 in the list does not make the range 10.)

items.q:
Heights of 6 sunflowers (cm):
152, 168, 147, 175, 160, 149
What is the range?
items.e: Highest 175 cm, lowest 147 cm. Range = 175 − 147 = 28 cm. (152 − 149 = 3 uses the first and last values, and 149 is not the lowest.)

items.q: Here are the ages of the players in a soccer team: 4 years, 10 years, 11 years, 10 years, 5 years, 4 years, 10 years, 14 years. What is the mode?
items.e: 10 appears 3 times, more than any other value. Mode: 10.

items.q: Here are the learners' marks out of 20: 8, 7, 14, 15, 17, 14. What is the range?
Here are the books read by learners this term: 15, 15, 15, 16, 15. What is the mode?
items.e: 15 appears 4 times, more than any other value. Mode: 15.

items.q:
Laps skated by 6 learners:
4, 9, 6, 3, 8, 10
What is the median?
items.e: In order: 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10. With 6 values there are two middle values, 6 and 8. The median is halfway between them: (6 + 8) ÷ 2 = 7. (4,5 uses 6 and 3 from the unordered list, and 14 forgets to divide by 2.)

items.q:
Ages of the swimmers in a lesson:
11, 14, 11, 16, 13, 11, 14
What is the mode?
items.e: 11 appears 3 times, more than any other age, so the mode is 11 years. (16 is the highest age, and 3 is how many times 11 appears.)

items.q:
Points scored by a basketball player in 7 games:
2, 4, 4, 6, 7, 7, 9
What is the mode?
items.e: 4 appears twice and 7 appears twice. Every other value appears once. So there are two modes: 4 and 7.

items.q:
Quiz scores out of 10:
8, 3, 6, 10, 5
What is the mode?
items.e: Each score appears only once, so no value appears most often. There is no mode. (10 is the highest score, and 5 is how many scores there are.)

items.q: Each X is one learner. What is the median number of pets?
items.e: There are 17 X’s, so the median is the 9th value in order. Count from the left: 3 learners have 0 pets, and the next 6 have 1 pet. The 9th value is 1. (2 is the middle of the number line, not of the data.)
The tallest stack is above 1, so the mode is 1 pet. (6 is the height of that stack, and 4 is the highest value.)

items.q:
Heights of 6 basketball players (cm):
152, 168, 147, 175, 160, 149
What is the range?
items.e: Highest 175 cm, lowest 147 cm. Range = 175 − 147 = 28 cm. (152 − 149 = 3 uses the first and last values, and 175 − 149 = 26 misses the lowest, 147.)

items.q: Here are the pumpkins sold each day at a farm stall: 13, 13, 14, 4, 10. What is the median?
items.e: In order: 4, 10, 13, 13, 14. The middle value is 13.

items.q: Here are the rainfall amounts on school days: 10 mm, 11 mm, 17 mm, 15 mm, 12 mm, 15 mm, 15 mm, 9 mm. What is the range?
Here are the pumpkins sold each day at a farm stall: 12, 19, 17, 23, 20, 19. What is the median?
items.e: In order: 12, 17, 19, 19, 20, 23. The middle value is 19.

items.q: Here are the pumpkins sold each day at a farm stall: 19, 13, 21, 21, 13, 19. What is the range?
Here are the books read by learners this term: 20, 21, 18, 11, 20. What is the range?
Here are the ages of the players in a soccer team: 22 years, 18 years, 16 years, 23 years, 11 years, 11 years, 15 years, 23 years. What is the median?
items.e: In order: 11, 11, 15, 16, 18, 22, 23, 23. The middle value is 17.

items.q: Here are the pumpkins sold each day at a farm stall: 8, 14, 14, 12, 7. What is the median?
items.e: In order: 7, 8, 12, 14, 14. The middle value is 12.

items.q: Here are the pumpkins sold each day at a farm stall: 18, 15, 13, 12, 20, 17, 21, 18, 20. What is the range?
Here are the learners' marks out of 20: 24, 18, 22, 11, 11, 19, 16, 22, 11. What is the mode?
items.e: 11 appears 3 times, more than any other value. Mode: 11.

items.q: Here are the pumpkins sold each day at a farm stall: 16, 14, 10, 15, 11, 8, 16, 10. What is the range?
Here are the rainfall amounts on school days: 8 mm, 10 mm, 18 mm, 16 mm, 9 mm. What is the range?
Here are the books read by learners this term: 11, 9, 11, 4, 4, 14, 3. What is the median?
items.e: In order: 3, 4, 4, 9, 11, 11, 14. The middle value is 9.

items.q: Here are the learners' marks out of 20: 6, 8, 6, 8, 7, 9, 6, 9, 13. What is the median?
items.e: In order: 6, 6, 6, 7, 8, 8, 9, 9, 13. The middle value is 8.
The tallest stack for 6A is above 8, so the mode is 8. (9 is how many learners scored 8, and 10 is the highest score.)
The tallest stack for 6B is above 9 (6 dots), so the mode is 9. (6 is how many learners scored 9.)
6A: highest 10, lowest 5. Range = 10 − 5 = 5. (9 − 1 = 8 uses the heights of the stacks.)
6B: highest 10, lowest 2. Range = 10 − 2 = 8. (5 is the range for 6A.)
The range measures how spread out the data is. 6B’s range (8) is bigger than 6A’s (5). The mode does not tell you about the spread.
8 or more means 8, 9 or 10: 3 + 6 + 3 = 12. (9 forgets the learners who scored exactly 8, and 16 is 6A.)

c: Both classes are spread out evenly
Both classes are bunched from 7 to 9
6A is bunched from 7 to 9; 6B is spread from 2 to 10
6A is spread from 2 to 10; 6B is bunched from 7 to 9
items.e: 6A: 6 + 9 + 5 = 20 of 25 dots are at 7, 8 or 9. 6B has dots all the way from 2 to 10, with the most at 9.

items.q:
Goals scored by two ringette teams in 6 games:
Lightning: 4, 6, 5, 7, 5, 3
Storm: 9, 2, 1, 8, 8, 2
What is the median for the Storm?
items.e: In order: 1, 2, 2, 8, 8, 9. The two middle values are 2 and 8: (2 + 8) ÷ 2 = 5. (4,5 uses 1 and 8 from the unordered list, and 10 forgets to divide by 2.)

items.q:
Goals scored by two ringette teams in 6 games:
Lightning: 4, 6, 5, 7, 5, 3
Storm: 9, 2, 1, 8, 8, 2
What is the mode for the Storm?
items.e: 2 appears twice and 8 appears twice, so the Storm has two modes: 2 and 8. (9 is the highest value.)

items.q:
Goals scored by two ringette teams in 6 games:
Lightning: 4, 6, 5, 7, 5, 3
Storm: 9, 2, 1, 8, 8, 2
Which conclusion is supported by the data?
c: Both teams average 5 goals a game
The Storm is better: it scored 9
items.e: Both teams scored 30 goals in 6 games, so both means are 5. One high game (9) does not make the Storm better, and the Storm scored 1 goal in one game.

items.q:
Laps skated in 10 minutes by learners in two gym classes:
6A: 14, 16, 15, 17, 16, 18, 16
6B: 12, 20, 15, 21, 11, 19, 14
What is the range for 6B?
items.e: Highest 21, lowest 11. Range = 21 − 11 = 10. (14 − 12 = 2 uses the last and first values, and 4 is the range for 6A.)

items.q:
Laps skated in 10 minutes by learners in two gym classes:
6A: 14, 16, 15, 17, 16, 18, 16
6B: 12, 20, 15, 21, 11, 19, 14
Which class has the higher median, and by how much?
items.e: 6A in order: 14, 15, 16, 16, 16, 17, 18, so its median is 16. 6B’s median is 15. 16 − 15 = 1 lap. (6 laps compares the ranges, 10 − 4.)

items.q: In which week were the two plants the same height?
items.e: The two lines start at the same point: both plants were 4 cm in week 1. After that, Plant A is always taller.

items.q: How much taller was Plant A than Plant B in week 5?
items.e: Week 5: Plant A is 26 cm and Plant B is 16 cm. 26 − 16 = 10 cm. (8 cm is the gap in week 4.)

items.q: Which plant grew faster?
c: Plant A: its line is steeper
Plant B: it grew more each week
Plant B: its line is lower
items.e: A steeper line means faster growth. Plant A grew 26 − 4 = 22 cm, and Plant B grew only 16 − 4 = 12 cm.

items.q:
Quiz scores out of 20:
Ethan: 18, 17, 19, 18, 3
Megan: 16, 16, 15, 17, 16
Who has the higher median?
items.e: Ethan in order: 3, 17, 18, 18, 19, so his median is 18. Megan in order: 15, 16, 16, 16, 17, so hers is 16.

items.q: How many learners voted for the science centre?
items.e: The bar reaches the line for 46. (6 is the height above the bottom of the scale, which starts at 40, not 0.)

items.q: How many more votes did the science centre get than the zoo?
items.e: 46 − 42 = 4 votes. (6 reads only the part of the bar above 40, and 2 is the zoo bar above 40.)

items.q: The science centre bar looks 3 times as tall. Did it get 3 times as many votes?
c: Yes: its bar is 3 times as tall
No: the zoo got more votes
items.e: 3 × 42 = 126, but the science centre got only 46 votes. The bars start at 40, so we see only 6 and 2 of the votes: that makes one look 3 times the other.

items.q: Why does this graph make the difference look big?
c: The bars are the same colour
items.e: When the scale starts at 40, the bottom part of every bar is cut off. The small difference (4 votes) then looks huge.
